## Summary

I've decomposed MAVSDK into **16 Logical Units** at `/out/manifest.json`:

**Domain units** (what the project is about): `mavsdk-session-core`, `mavlink-protocol-dispatch`, `mavlink-parameter-protocol`, `mavlink-ftp-protocol`, `mavlink-mission-transfer`, `vehicle-command-plugins`, `raw-mavlink-plugins`, `mission-safety-plugins`, `telemetry-sensing-plugins`, `camera-gimbal-plugins`, `file-transfer-plugins`, `vehicle-config-plugins`

**Infra units** (how it talks to the world): `mavlink-transport-io`, `http-download-utility`, `core-cache-utilities`, `mavsdk-grpc-server`

The 37 individual plugin directories were grouped into 7 thematic domain units by what they let a caller *do* (command in real time, plan autonomously, observe passively, control payload imaging, move files, configure the vehicle, or bypass the typed API), rather than one unit per plugin or one giant unit — each grouping was verified by a dedicated scout that read the actual source and traced real call sites.

**Excluded** (with reasons): vendored third-party deps, all tests, docs, build tooling, and — notably — the entire `c/`, `jni/`, and `py/` client-binding trees, which are mechanically generated from the proto interface by codegen scripts rather than independently authored logic.

**Known limitations**, recorded in `violations_observed`: the `depends_on` edges use a curated, class-level entrypoint per unit rather than enumerating every fine-grained accessor call plugins make into `SystemImpl`/`ServerComponentImpl`, so some real call-graph edges are simplified rather than individually listed.
